items.good: The document follows the template's headings in order: a title naming the product, an opening saying how it is put together with a link to the README where the UX and its words are defined, the principles each in a line (with a line saying there is no base architecture to link), User stories in the 'As a user, I want' form, Architecture with a Logical view holding one SVG figure shown as an image and the lines it cannot show, a Physical view holding a tree and the dependency and start lines, and Test. Each list line is one sentence, its why after a blank line indented under it, and nothing is bold. The figure has a box for each component holding its name alone, a legend telling code from AI from person from files on disk, a dashed frame round the one Python file, a labelled arrow from each component to what it acts on, and dark-mode colours; I computed every arrow against every other arrow and every box and none crosses another or runs through a box. Test has no project rules to link, and says so in place of the link before giving what this tool's checks need.

From the opening I can tell how the tool is put together: one Python script in which a Planner decides where each file goes or why it stays, a Mover carries that out while a Record keeper keeps each move outside the folder, and an Undoer puts back the last move. The terms are linked to the README. Line 9 says there is no base architecture, so every principle is its own. Each principle is one line, and each is a rule the decisions are held to rather than a means: never delete, rename or overwrite; move only the files directly in the folder; add nothing inside the folder but the kinds' folders; decide where each file goes in one place; install by downloading one file.

Every scene of the README rests on a story, each one command the user runs at the tool's edge: the run with no option that lists, on ~/Downloads or another folder (README 29-43, 90-95) -> story 1; --move (README 45-68) -> story 2; --undo (README 70-88) -> story 3; --help after installing (README 182-186) -> story 4. No story is a step inside the tool, none repeats another, and none is named by a technology.

The figure and the first line beside it show how each story is achieved, in order. List: Command line asks the Planner, which reads the names in the folder and its kinds' folders, and then prints a line per file. Move: the same plan is handed to the Mover, which makes missing kinds' folders, moves the files and has the Record keeper add each move to the Record; the Command line then prints what became of each file. Undo: the Undoer reads the last move through the Record keeper, moves the files back and removes the kinds' folders it left empty. Help: the Command line prints usage. The choices a reader would question each come with their why: recording each move as it is made, moving by hard link instead of rename, the copy path on FAT/exFAT, removing folders only after the files are back, and one record per folder. Each box holds only a component's name, and no component or path duplicates another.

The tree places all five components in the one Python 3 script (standard library only), the tests as Python unittest files, the installed script in ~/.local/bin, and the Record keeper's folder on Linux and on macOS, with the record as a JSON Lines file named by a hash of the folder's path. Each place has its kind beside it. The lines below the tree say the tool depends only on Python and its standard library, in the version the README's Requirements give (3.8, README 124). They also say it is started as `organize-downloads`, whose first line hands it to python3, and how the home, Downloads and record places are found.

The section says the project has no rules for checks to link, and gives in their place what this tool's checks need. Code components are tested with unittest, each test a Given/When/Then that loads the script as a module. The user stories are tested by running the script on a temporary folder with a temporary home. Everything runs by one command from the repository root on Linux, and on macOS the user runs the tool once. I built a throwaway script without the .py extension and a tests folder in a mktemp folder. Loading the script with SourceFileLoader and running `python3 -m unittest discover organize-downloads/tests` from its root works (2 tests, OK). Run in the real repository today, the command fails with 'Start directory is not importable', because the tests folder does not exist yet at this design stage. That is the folder the tree says the builder makes. No case inputs or pass bars are written.

items.did: I checked each line against the principles and against each other. I also checked the claims in a mktemp folder with Python: os.link to a name that is taken raises FileExistsError and leaves that file as it was; os.open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL on a taken name raises FileExistsError; os.rename replaces the file at the target. All three hold. I then followed a move run in which the Mover makes a missing kind's folder and then cannot move the file into it. Lines 56-58 and 60-67 design for exactly this: a hard link that fails because a file came to hold the name after the Planner looked, or a copy that fails on a full FAT/exFAT drive.
items.lacking: Lines 45-47 say each move and each kind's folder made is added to the record, and that the first of these in a run starts the record anew. So a run whose only success is making a kind's folder replaces the folder's record with one that holds just that folder and no moved file. That conflicts with three other statements. Line 5-6 defines the folder's last move as 'the last run that moved a file in it'. Lines 50-51 say 'a run that moves nothing leaves the record of the last move as it was, so an undo after it still puts back the files of the last move'. README 5-6 says the tool undoes 'its last run that moved files in that folder'. After such a run, --undo puts back none of the files the real last move took. A builder has to pick one of these lines and break the other.

items.good: Each line is a decision that would change what was approved if it changed: the principles; the order the components act in; recording as each move is made; hard link instead of rename; the copy path on drives without hard links; removing folders after the files are back; one record per folder; the place and form of the record; the dependency and how the tool is started; how home and the system are found; how the components and the stories are checked, by which command and on which systems. Behaviour per case (what stays and why, the extension table) is left to the README and the tests. Python's version is pointed to in the README rather than repeated, and the document records no history and no status.

Reading once from the top, I understood each line where I met it. Words of the UX such as a kind's folder are linked in the opening to the README, and the README link resolves. The folder's last move is defined where it is first used, and a hard link is explained in the line that uses it. Each component keeps one name throughout the text, the figure and the tree. The Record keeper (the component) and the record or Record (the file on disk) are kept apart. No other product is named without saying what it is, and no line rests on a reason given only later.
